opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and one we think about a lot. Imitation is a very powerful starting point, because human driving data captures an enormous amount of implicit knowledge: how to merge, how to negotiate at a four-way stop, how to be appropriately assertive without being rude. But "drive like a human" isn't actually the objective. Humans are distracted, they speed, they get tired, and the data is full of behavior you don't want to reproduce. So imitation gets you a prior on what reasonable driving looks like, but it doesn't tell you what *good* driving is.

The way I think about it, good driving has a few layers. The first and non-negotiable one is safety: avoid collisions, and also avoid creating situations where others have to take evasive action to avoid you. That second part is subtle. You can be technically collision-free but still drive in a way that pushes risk onto other people.

The second layer is following the rules of the road, but with judgment. Traffic law is the baseline, yet real driving needs some flexibility. If a truck is double-parked, you may need to cross a double yellow line carefully. A good driver knows when the rules bend and when they don't.

The third layer is what I'd call social compatibility. Being predictable and legible to others matters a lot. If other drivers and pedestrians can't read your intent, even safe maneuvers cause confusion. So you want the vehicle to behave in a way people naturally understand, neither overly timid, which actually creates its own hazards and frustrates people, nor overly aggressive.

And then there's comfort and progress: smooth driving, reaching your destination efficiently, and not stopping for no reason.

The challenge is that these objectives trade off against each other, and they're very hard to write down as a single hand-crafted cost function. So a lot of the interesting work is combining learning from demonstrations with additional signals: reward models, rule-based evaluators, and preference-style feedback about which of two behaviors is better. That's similar in spirit to what's happened with large language models, where you pretrain on lots of data and then align the model toward what you actually want.

Evaluation is a big part of this too. You need closed-loop simulation with realistic agents that react to you, because open-loop metrics, like how closely you matched the logged human trajectory, can be quite misleading. The human might have done one perfectly fine thing, and your model might do a different but equally good, or even better, thing. So ultimately, defining good driving means building scalable ways to judge behavior across lots of scenarios, especially the rare and hard ones in the long tail, not just measuring how closely you copy people.

r001.rationale: The response defines good driving through safety, rule-following, social compatibility, comfort, and progress, then separately discusses learning signals and closed-loop evaluation to train and assess whether a model meets those goals.

r002.rationale: It presents following traffic rules as a layer of good driving and contrasts that with imitation, which it describes as only a prior that does not define the objective.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and it's really one of the central questions in the field right now. Imitation is a wonderful starting point. Humans are actually pretty good drivers most of the time, and we have an enormous amount of data of people driving, so learning to behave like a human gets you remarkably far. But imitation alone has some fundamental limits.

The first is that humans are not perfect. If you just imitate, you inherit the mistakes along with the good behavior: distraction, speeding, tailgating, running yellow lights a little late. We don't want the model to learn that the goal is to be average. We want it to be better than the average human, and ideally better than the best human.

The second issue is coverage. Human driving data is dominated by uneventful situations. The cases that matter most for safety, the near misses, the pedestrian stepping out from behind a bus, are extremely rare in the data, and often when they happen, the human response is not the one you'd want to copy. So you can't rely on imitation to teach you the long tail.

So the way we think about it is that imitation gives you a prior, a sense of what reasonable, natural, predictable driving looks like, and then you need other signals layered on top. Some of that is explicit: we can define measures of safety, like keeping appropriate buffers from other agents, respecting traffic rules, being comfortable for the passengers, not braking harshly, and being predictable so other road users can anticipate you. Some of it is learned from outcomes, through simulation and closed-loop evaluation, where we can ask: given this situation, did the behavior lead to a collision or a near collision, and could a different action have avoided it?

And the key insight is that these two things pull against each other sometimes. The safest behavior in isolation is to not move at all, and that's obviously useless. A good driver is one who is safe and also makes progress, blends into traffic, and behaves in ways other humans find intuitive. So defining good driving ends up being about balancing a set of objectives, and a lot of our work goes into making that balance explicit, measurable, and something we can hold the model accountable to, rather than hoping it falls out of copying people.

r001.rationale: The response discusses defining good driving and evaluating behavior, but does not clearly distinguish specifying the definition from ensuring the system satisfies it.

r002.rationale: It lists explicit safety measures and traffic rules, but presents them as signals layered on imitation, not as an alternative to imitation for specifying good driving.

astra-6.text:
I think imitation is a useful starting point, but it’s not the definition of good driving. Human drivers make mistakes, and they have different styles. So you need to ask what you actually want the system to accomplish: make safe progress, follow the rules of the road, be comfortable for passengers, and behave predictably around other road users.

Those objectives can be in tension. Braking hard might be the right thing to do to avoid a collision, but you don’t want a system that brakes hard every time there’s uncertainty. And being excessively cautious can create problems for other drivers, too. The challenge is to understand the situation well enough to make an appropriate decision, including recognizing what you don’t know.

So I’d look beyond whether the model chose the same trajectory as a human. What happens when you let its decisions play out? Does it maintain a safe margin? Does it handle an unexpected action by another road user? Can it make progress without forcing others to react abruptly? That kind of evaluation is essential, because driving is an interaction, not just a sequence of predictions.

r001.rationale: The response names desired driving objectives, then separately calls for evaluating what happens when the model’s decisions play out to see whether it meets them.

r002.rationale: It includes following road rules as one objective, but does not propose explicit driving rules as an alternative specification to imitation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think imitation is a very useful starting point, but it’s not the definition of good driving. Human drivers make mistakes, and they have different habits, so you need to ask what behavior you actually want the system to produce.

Safety is central, of course, but you also want to make progress, be comfortable for passengers, and be predictable to other road users. Those objectives interact. Braking very aggressively might avoid a particular conflict, but anticipating that conflict and slowing down smoothly is better driving.

So I think about it in terms of evaluating the consequences of the model’s decisions over time. Does it maintain appropriate margins? Does it handle uncertainty well? Does it interact sensibly with pedestrians and other vehicles? You need closed-loop evaluation, where the vehicle’s actions affect what happens next, rather than just asking whether its predicted trajectory matches a human’s recorded trajectory. There can be several good ways to navigate a situation, and matching one demonstration doesn’t tell you whether you’ve learned to drive well.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes imitation from the broader definition of good driving, but does not distinguish defining that standard from ensuring the system satisfies it.

r002.rationale: It names objectives such as safety, comfort, and predictability, but does not propose explicit driving rules as an alternative to imitation.
